title: Hash Tables: Computing the Address
objective: By the end of this lesson you will understand how hash tables work and know when to use them.
complexity: Average case O of 1 for insert, lookup and delete. Worst case O of n when all keys collide in one bucket. Space O of n.
challenge: If your table has four slots and you insert a thousand keys, what happens to lookup time, and what should the table do about it?

analogy.name: Theatre coat check
analogy.mapping: Your coat is the value, your ticket number is the hash of your key, and the numbered hook is the array slot. The attendant never searches the rack; the number tells them exactly where to reach.

mistakes: Using a mutable object as a key, or changing a key after it is stored, so its hash no longer points to its bucket.
Assuming a hash table preserves insertion order or is sorted.
Never resizing, so buckets grow into long chains and lookups degrade to linear time.
Assuming Python's hash of a string is stable across separate program runs.

acts.heading: One Million Names, One Lookup
acts.narration: Imagine a phone book with a million names, and you need one number, right now.

beats.narration: Scanning name by name could take a million comparisons. Even sorted, binary search still needs about twenty steps. Can we do it in one?
beats.visual: A long vertical list of names; a magnifying glass crawls down it, counter ticking up to 1,000,000, then a binary search version halving the list with a counter stopping at 20.

beats.narration: Hash tables get you there. One jump, no searching. Here is the trick.
beats.visual: The list collapses into a short row of numbered boxes; a single glowing arrow leaps directly into one box, counter reading 1.

acts.heading: The Coat Check Trick
acts.narration: Think about the coat check at a theatre.

beats.narration: You hand over your coat and get ticket forty two. Later the attendant does not search every hook. The number is the location.
beats.visual: A person hands a coat over a counter, receives a ticket stamped 42, and the attendant walks straight to hook 42 on a numbered rack.

beats.narration: A hash table does the same thing. It turns your key, like a word, into a number, and that number is a shelf position. Computing beats searching.
beats.visual: The word "cat" flows into a small machine labelled hash, a number pops out, and an arrow drops into slot 2 of a numbered array.

acts.heading: Hash, Modulo, Jump
acts.narration: So how do we turn a word into a shelf number?

beats.narration: A hash function chews up the key and spits out a big integer. Same key in, same number out, every time.
beats.visual: Letters of "cat" feed into a gear-filled box; a large number 312 emerges. The word is fed again and the same 312 appears.

beats.narration: Take that number modulo the number of slots, the remainder after dividing, and you get an index inside the array.
beats.visual: 312 divided by 4 shown as division, remainder 0 highlighted, and an arrow pointing at slot 0 of a four-slot array.

beats.narration: Store the key and value there. To look it up, hash again and jump straight to that slot. No scanning.
beats.visual: A key-value tile drops into slot 0; then a lookup arrow re-hashes and lands on slot 0 with a green check.

beats.narration: But two different keys can land in the same slot. That is a collision, and it is completely normal. Each slot holds a small list, and we scan only that tiny list.
beats.visual: A second tile aims at slot 0, the slot expands into a chain of two linked tiles, and a tiny arrow walks the chain of two.

beats.narration: Keep the array roomy, and those chains stay about one item long, so lookups stay constant time.
beats.visual: The array grows from four slots to eight; long chains redistribute into single tiles across the wider array.

acts.heading: Building One in Python
acts.narration: Let us build a tiny hash table in Python and watch it work.

beats.narration: Four empty buckets, a hash made by summing letter codes, and two functions: put and get.
beats.visual: Code panel on the left, a four-slot bucket diagram on the right, all buckets empty.

beats.narration: Watch cat and act collide, share a bucket, and still be found correctly.
beats.visual: Two tiles labelled cat and act both flying toward bucket 0, forming a chain that a lookup arrow walks.

acts.heading: Recap and Challenge
acts.narration: Intuition first: do not search for the address, compute it.

beats.narration: Hash the key, take the remainder, jump to the bucket, scan its short chain. Average insert and lookup are O of one. Worst case, if every key collides, O of n.
beats.visual: Four-step flow diagram: key, hash number, modulo, bucket. Beside it, average O of 1 in green and worst case O of n in red.

beats.narration: Common traps: changing a key after storing it, assuming the order of items is stable, and trusting hash values to be the same across program runs. Now a challenge. If your table has four slots and you store a thousand keys, what happens to lookup time, and what should the table do about it?
beats.visual: Three warning cards fading in, then a four-slot table drowning under enormous chains with a question mark above it.

lines: i = sum(ord(c) for c in key) % len(table)
i = sum(ord(c) for c in key) % len(table)

walkthrough.narration: We create a table of four empty buckets.
Storing cat. Its letter codes sum to 312, and 312 modulo 4 is 0.
Bucket zero is empty, so we append the pair cat nine.
Now act. Same letters, same sum, same slot zero. A collision.
We scan the bucket. The pair there has key cat, which is not act.
No match, so act four joins the same bucket as a chain.
Looking up act. Hash again, land straight on bucket zero.
First pair is cat. Not what we want, keep walking the chain.
Second pair matches act, so we return four and print it.
Looking up cat hits bucket zero and matches on the very first pair, printing nine.
